ir_stages.name: Preparation
ir_stages.description: Establish a plan of action in the event of a DDoS attack on the company network.

checklist.text: Develop and document incident response procedures
Conduct incident response training and drills (tabletop/Red vs Blue)

ir_stages.name: Detection & Analysis
ir_stages.description: Detect, analyze, and determine the scope of an incident. Active EOC Monitoring of the situation.

ir_stages.name: Containment
ir_stages.description: Stop the attack and limit its scope and impact. Isolate ports and services quarantining the network. Collection of evidence for post attack.

checklist.text: Block malicious IP addresses and domains

ir_stages.name: Eradication
ir_stages.description: Remove the threat and restore systems to a known good state. Back up statuses and locations.

checklist.text: Rebuild systems from clean media if necessary
Establish rules to prevent excessive packet transmission. Snort rule refinement.

ir_stages.name: Recovery
ir_stages.description: Restore systems to normal operations and verify they function correctly.

checklist.text: Restore data from clean backups if neccessary

dr_stages.name: Prevention
dr_stages.description: Implement preventive measures to avoid disasters.

checklist.text: Test backup and recovery procedures regularly
Verify back up status and locations

dr_stages.name: Detection
dr_stages.description: Detect when a disaster has occurred. Active IDS/IPS.

checklist.text: Establish alerting for critical service failures

dr_stages.name: Recovery
dr_stages.description: Restore systems and services to operational status.

checklist.text: Document recovery time and RTO/RPO achievement

dr_stages.name: Post-Recovery
dr_stages.description: Restore full operations and improve resilience. Verification of rule sets for IDS/IPS and blocked IP addresses.

## Table‑top Exercise Scenario **ThreeBlindArchitects – Cyber‑Incident Response Exercise** --- ### 1. Scenario Title **“The Silent Surge: A Ransomware Campaign Unfolds in the Infrastructure Core”** --- ### 2. Background | Element | Details | |---------|---------| | **Organization** | **ThreeBlindArchitects** – a mid‑size technology consultancy (≈ 350 employees) that designs, builds, and maintains custom software solutions for Fortune‑500 clients. | | **Critical Systems** | • **Web Servers** – public‑facing services (CMS, API gateway, support portal).
• **Local Maintenance Machines** – internal dev‑test servers, build agents, and a dedicated “maintenance” workstation used for firmware updates and network diagnostics.
• **Network Infrastructure** – core routers, Layer‑3 switches, enterprise firewalls, and SD‑WAN endpoints.
• **Storage** – shared SAN (10 TB) containing code repositories, databases, and backup media. | | **Threat Landscape** | • Advanced persistent threat (APT) activity targeting tech firms.
• Supply‑chain attacks via third‑party firmware and software bundles.
• Increasing use of ransomware‑as‑a‑service platforms.
• Phishing campaigns leveraging “trusted vendor” domains. | | **Current Security Posture** | • Perimeter firewalls with IDS/IPS.
• Network segmentation: DMZ, internal network, and isolated maintenance VLAN.
• Endpoint protection on all servers.
• 30‑day backup window, nightly full snapshot to off‑site storage.
• No formal ransomware‑response playbook documented. | --- ### 3. Inject Timeline (5 Injects) | Inject # | Time | Event & Description | Information Provided to Participants | Expected Actions / Questions | |----------|------|---------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------| | **Inject 1** | **08:00** | **Unusual Web Traffic Spike** – External monitoring reports a 250 % surge in HTTP requests, many of which contain malformed URLs (e.g., `/../../etc/passwd`). The web servers log a high rate of 404 errors. | • Web server logs (last 30 min).
• Firewall alert: “High HTTP request rate from IP 203.0.113.45”.
• Incident response team receives notification. | • Verify if traffic is legitimate (e.g., DDoS).
• Is the anomaly tied to a known campaign?
• Should we block the source IP or throttle traffic? | | **Inject 2** | **10:00** | **Compromised Maintenance Machine** – Security Operations Center (SOC) receives an alert: the local maintenance workstation (MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E) is attempting outbound HTTPS traffic to a new domain (`malware-update.example.com`). | • Process list and network connection details from the machine.
• External DNS record for `malware-update.example.com` (IP 198.51.100.23).
• Email from internal vendor support stating “Please update firmware to version 5.2.3”. | • Is the maintenance machine compromised or is the vendor communication legitimate?
• Should we isolate the device immediately?
• How does this impact the network? | | **Inject 3** | **12:00** | **Unauthorized Network Device** – Network monitoring shows a new MAC address (AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF) connected to the core router. Port scan activity detected on ports 21, 22, 80, 443. | • Router logs indicating new device on port Gig0/1.
• ARP table entry for the unknown MAC.
• Traffic flow report showing outbound traffic from the device to IP 203.0.113.45. | • Identify the device (spoofed or rogue).
• Are there any VLAN segmentation breaches?
• Should we quarantine the port or disable the device? | | **Inject 4** | **14:00** | **Ransomware on Storage** – Backup system alerts that a nightly snapshot failed. On investigation, multiple files on the SAN show a new extension `.locked`. The backup job logs a 100 % failure rate. | • File integrity logs: list of encrypted files, hash changes.
• Ransom note displayed on a random workstation.
• Ransom demand: “Pay 5 BTC within 48 hrs to decrypt”. | • Confirm scope of encryption (is it isolated or widespread).
• Evaluate backup integrity and restoration options.
• Decide whether to pay or pursue legal/communication avenues. | | **Inject 5** | **16:00** | **External Data Breach Notice** – CFO receives an email from a former employee’s compromised account: “Your internal database has been accessed. We have copies of all client PII.” The email includes a link to a download of a data dump (10 GB). | • Email header details (From, To, IP).
• Link to a file-sharing service (malicious URL).
• Notification that the internal firewall blocked the connection but logs show the IP. | • Determine if data exfiltration occurred.
• Notify legal and PR teams.
• Initiate incident response escalation and client notification plan. | --- ### 4. Discussion Questions 1. **Detection & Initial Response** - Which monitoring tools should have detected the early signs of compromise (web traffic spike, unauthorized device) earlier? - What are the pros and cons of hard‑blocking the source IP versus throttling/ rate‑limiting? 2. **Containment & Isolation** - How should we prioritize isolating the compromised maintenance machine versus shutting down the entire maintenance VLAN? - What network segmentation policies could prevent a rogue device from reaching core switches? 3. **Investigation & Attribution** - What indicators (IP reputation, domain age, command‑and‑control signatures) would help attribute the attack to a known threat actor? - Should we involve external threat intelligence feeds at this stage? 4. **Recovery & Restoration** - How do we assess the integrity of backups before restoring from them? - What procedures should be followed to avoid restoring encrypted or compromised data? 5. **Legal, Regulatory & Communication** - Under which data‑breach notification laws (e.g., GDPR, CCPA) must we notify clients and regulators? - What internal/external communication strategy should we employ to mitigate reputational damage? 6. **Post‑Incident Lessons & Improvements** - What gaps in our current security controls were exposed by this exercise? - How can we formalize a ransomware response playbook and integrate it into our annual SOC playbook review? 7. **Financial & Vendor Considerations** - What criteria should we use to decide whether to pay a ransom? - How do we assess the legitimacy of firmware update requests from third‑party vendors? 8. **Operational Continuity** - How can we maintain service availability for critical web services while containment and recovery are underway? - What failover or cloud‑based options exist for our SAN in a crisis? 9. **Cyber‑Insurance & Claim Process** - What information must we gather to file a cyber‑insurance claim promptly? - Are there any exclusions we should be aware of for ransomware incidents? 10. **Training & Awareness** - How can we incorporate lessons learned into employee training programs, particularly for those handling maintenance machines? - What phishing simulation metrics should we track post‑exercise to gauge improvement? --- ### 5. Suggested Exercise Duration & Logistics - **Total Time**: 3–4 hours (including debrief). - **Participants**: SOC analysts, network engineers, system administrators, legal counsel, PR, executive leadership. - **Facilitator Role**: Introduce each inject, provide materials, monitor discussion, record decisions. - **Debrief Focus**: Decision points, gaps identified, action items, and timeline for implementing improvements. --- **End of Scenario**

## Incident Simulation Scenario – ThreeBlindArchitects *(Technology Sector – Web Services & Internal Infrastructure)* --- ### 1. Incident Overview | Item | Description | |------|-------------| | **Incident Type** | Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) + Ransomware & Data Exfiltration | | **Threat Actor** | “Black Orchid” – a well‑known threat group targeting architectural firms for proprietary designs and intellectual property. | | **Primary Motivation** | 1) Leak architectural drawings to competitors. 2) Ransom for full access to confidential CAD files. | | **Detection Medium** | SIEM alerts, user reports, and an internal honeypot that captured a malicious payload. | | **Scope** | Web servers, local maintenance machines (DevOps & Support), core network infrastructure, and storage arrays. | --- ### 2. Attack Timeline (24‑hour window) | Time (UTC) | Activity | Notes | |------------|----------|-------| | **00:00** | **Initial Compromise** – Phishing email with macro‑enabled DOCX delivers a malicious Office payload. | Recipient: Senior Architect (user = `jdoe`). | | **00:12** | **Execution on Endpoint** – Macro installs a PowerShell script that downloads a backdoor from `malicious.com`. | PowerShell runs silently, creates `WinRM.exe` service. | | **00:18** | **C2 Command & Control** – The backdoor contacts `185.23.67.101:4444`. | C2 uses custom TLS‑encrypted protocol. | | **00:30** | **Privilege Escalation** – Exploit “Zero‑Day Credential Dumping” (`CVE‑2024‑XXXXX`) to extract domain admin credentials. | Credentials stored in encrypted registry hive. | | **01:00** | **Lateral Movement** – Using stolen creds, attacker logs into Web server cluster (`web01`, `web02`). | Executes a scheduled task to install reverse shell. | | **01:15** | **Data Access** – Attacker copies CAD files (`*.dwg`, `*.pdf`) to an internal staging folder on `web01`. | | **01:45** | **Ransomware Deployment** – `cryptor.exe` is dropped onto `web01` and `web02`. | Targets `\\storage.local\shared\CAD`. | | **02:00** | **Encryption & Ransom Note** – All files in `\\storage.local\shared\CAD` are encrypted. Ransom note placed in `C:\ransom.txt`. | | **02:15** | **Exfiltration Phase 1** – Small subset of key drawings exfiltrated via HTTP POST to `data.exfil.com`. | | **03:00** | **Exfiltration Phase 2** – Large batch of design files pushed via SFTP to attacker’s staging server (IP 202.48.3.77). | | **04:00** | **Internal Recon** – Attacker maps network using Nmap from compromised `web01`. | | **04:30** | **Persistence** – Adds `web01` to scheduled tasks list; creates hidden service on `devops01`. | | **05:00** | **Backup Tampering** – Modifies `bkp_schedule` on Storage array to delete latest full backup snapshot. | | **05:30** | **Deception** – Generates benign logs to cover traces, then initiates “clean‑up” scripts on `web02`. | | **06:00** | **Alert Received** – SIEM flags anomalous outbound traffic from `web01` to unknown IP. | | **06:15** | **IR Team Mobilized** – Incident Commander (IC) convenes playbook. | --- ### 3. Affected Systems | System | Role | Status (post‑attack) | |--------|------|----------------------| | **Web01 / Web02** | Public‑facing architecture portfolio & client portal | Compromised, ransomware active | | **DevOps01** | Local maintenance & build automation | Lateral foothold, hidden service | | **Support01** | Local maintenance machine for field technicians | Compromised, scheduled task created | | **Router01 / Switch01** | Core network infrastructure | Normal, but infected traffic observed | | **Storage Array (NAS01)** | Central file store (`\\storage.local\shared`) | Encrypted CAD files, backup snapshot deleted | | **Backup Server (BKP01)** | Off‑site backup | Snapshot deletion flagged | --- ### 4. Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) | Category | IoC | Description | |----------|-----|-------------| | **Malicious Domains** | `malicious.com` | C2 domain used by the backdoor. | | **Malicious IPs** | `185.23.67.101` (C2) | Outbound TLS to port 4444. | | | `202.48.3.77` (attacker’s SFTP) | Large file uploads. | | **File Hashes** | SHA‑256: `3b2d8e…` (cryptor.exe) | Ransomware binary. | | | SHA‑256: `9f6c1a…` (PowerShell script) | Initial payload. | | **Registry Keys** | `HKLM\Software\WinRM` | Custom service created by backdoor. | | | `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` | Persistence task on `web01`. | | **Process Names** | `WinRM.exe`, `cryptor.exe`, `ransom.txt` | Malicious processes. | | **Network Patterns** | 5 GB of outbound traffic to port 22 (SFTP) within 24 h | Exfiltration. | | | > 10 HTTP POSTs to `data.exfil.com` | Small data exfil. | | **User Accounts** | `jdoe`, `admin`, `svc_web` | Compromised credentials. | | **Backup Anomalies** | Deletion of snapshot `bkp-2026-04-13-00` | Backup tampering. | --- ### 5. Incident Response Plan – Phase‑by‑Phase Actions | Phase | Objective | Expected Actions (IR Team) | |-------|-----------|----------------------------| | **5.1 Preparation** | Ensure playbook, contacts, and tools are ready. | • Review IR playbook.
• Verify forensic imaging tools.
• Confirm communication channels (internal & external). | | **5.2 Identification** | Detect, classify, and confirm the incident. | • SIEM alert triage.
• Check event logs on `web01`, `web02`, `devops01`.
• Validate IoCs (domain, IP, hashes).
• Notify stakeholders (CISO, legal, PR). | | **5.3 Containment** | Stop further spread and preserve evidence. | • Disable network access for `web01`, `web02` (apply ACL on Router01).
• Isolate compromised endpoints (PowerShell remoting blocked).
• Remove malicious scheduled tasks & services.
• Snapshot disk images for forensic analysis. | | **5.4 Eradication** | Remove threat artifacts. | • Delete `cryptor.exe`, `WinRM.exe`, malicious registry keys.
• Restore services to pre‑compromise state.
• Apply latest OS and application patches (especially CVE‑2024‑XXXXX).
• Reset compromised credentials; enforce MFA. | | **5.5 Recovery** | Return systems to production safely. | • Decrypt unaffected files (if backup available).
• Deploy latest backups to `NAS01` (restore last good snapshot).
• Re‑image compromised hosts and rebuild from known good images.
• Validate integrity of restored data (checksum comparison). | | **5.6 Lessons Learned** | Capture insights and improve defenses. | • Conduct a post‑mortem with all stakeholders.
• Update playbooks: include new IoCs, detection rules, and mitigation steps.
• Run a red‑team/blue‑team drill based on this scenario.
• Issue mandatory security training (phishing, credential hygiene). | --- ### 6. Disaster Recovery (DR) Steps 1. **Failover to Secondary Web Farm** - Route external DNS to secondary cluster (`web02‑backup`). - Verify SSL certificates and load balancer health checks. 2. **Backup Restoration** - Retrieve last clean snapshot (`bkp-2026-04-13-00`) from off‑site storage. - Restore CAD files to `\\storage.local\shared\CAD`. - Validate checksum of all critical files. 3. **Data Validation & Integrity Checks** - Run `checksum` tool on all CAD files. - Confirm that no encrypted files remain. 4. **Re‑integration** - Re‑enable compromised endpoints after clean‑image. - Apply network segmentation changes (e.g., separate DevOps VLAN). 5. **Business Continuity** - Ensure clients have access to updated portfolios via temporary CDN. - Offer client notification and support hotline for any data concerns. --- ### 7. Key Take‑aways & Next Steps | Item | Action | |------|--------| | **Zero‑Day CVE Exploit** | Patch management policy review – implement “Just‑in‑Time” patching. | | **Phishing Delivery** | Enhance user awareness training; enable attachment sandboxing. | | **Backdoor Persistence** | Deploy host‑based intrusion detection and process whitelisting. | | **Backup Tampering** | Enforce immutable backup snapshots; audit backup logs daily. | | **Data Exfiltration** | Deploy data‑loss prevention (DLP) for CAD file types. | --- **Prepared by:** Cybersecurity Incident Response Team – ThreeBlindArchitects **Date:** 2026‑04‑14 10:00 UTC ---
